facts.text: Civil Appeal No. 695 of 1965 filed in Supreme Court.

anchor.surface_text: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION Civil Appeal No, 695 of 1965.

facts.text: Appeal by special leave from judgment and order dated June 17, 18, 1964 of Gujarat High Court in Civil Revision Application No. 430 of 1961.

anchor.surface_text: Appeal by special leave from the judgment and order dated June 17, 18, 1964 of the Gujarat High Court in Civil Revision Application No. 430 of 1961.

facts.text: Suit brought by respondents Nos. 1 and 2 against appellant and three others in Court of Judge Small Causes at Ahmedabad under s. 28 of Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947.

anchor.surface_text: A suit was brought by respondents Nos. 1 and 2  hereinafter referred to as the respondents  against the appellant and three Others in the Court of Judge Small Causes at Ahmedabad, under s. 28 of the Bombay Rents.

facts.text: Defendants Nos. 1 to 3 were tenants-in-chief of the premises, appellant was defendant No. 4 their sub-tenant.

anchor.surface_text: The case of the respondents was that the other three persons who were defendants Nos. 1 to 3 were the tenants-in-chief of the premises while the present appellant who was defendant No. 4 was their sub- tenant.

facts.text: Respondents gave notice to tenants-in-chief terminating tenancy to vacate after November 30, 1956.

anchor.surface_text: The respondents had given notice to the tenants-in- chief terminating the tenancy and asked them to vacate the premises from after November 30, 1956, which was the end of the month of tenancy.

facts.text: Suit filed on March 1, 1957.

anchor.surface_text: The suit was filed on March 1, 1957 and was based on two grounds, namely,

facts.text: Suit based on grounds of rent unpaid for six months and unlawful sub-letting by tenants-in-chief to appellant.

anchor.surface_text: The suit was filed on March 1, 1957 and was based on two grounds, namely,  i  that the rent had not been paid for six months, and  ii  that there had been unlawful sub-letting by the tenants-in-chief to the appellant.

facts.text: Defendant No. 1 defended that premises taken by firm consisting of three defendants, but later no longer partner.

anchor.surface_text: One of them took the defence that the premises had been taken by a firm at a time when it consisted of the three defendants. But later defendant No. 1 no longer remained a partner of the firm and had nothing to do with the premises

facts.text: Defendants Nos. 2 and 3 contended rent Rs. 26 excessive, prayed standard rent fixation; defendant No. 1 no longer partner, defendant No. 4 became partner; denied sub-letting; rent deposited, no arrears.

anchor.surface_text: Defendants Nos. 2 and 3 on the other hand contended that the rent claimed  i.e., Rs. 26  was excessive and prayed that standard rent should be fixed for the premises. These defendants further said that defendant No. 1 was no longer a partner of the firm and that in his place defendant No. 4  i.e., the present appellant  had become partner.

facts.text: Appellant denied being sub-tenant; claimed entire interest of defendants 1-3 transferred to him, he is tenant; arrears paid into court.

anchor.surface_text: The appellant also filed a written-statement. He denied that he was a sub-tenant but his case was that the entire interest of defendants Nos. 1 to 3 in the business along with the interest in the premises had been transferred to him and he was thus the tenant of the respondents and not a sub-tenant,

facts.text: Trial court held defendants 1-3 not in arrears.

anchor.surface_text: On these pleadings, the trial court framed four issues. The first issue was whether defendants Nos. 1 to 3 were in arrears and it was held that they were not in arrears.

facts.text: Trial court held standard rent is contractual rent Rs. 26 per mensem.

anchor.surface_text: The second issue was about the standard rent of the premises and the trial court held that it was the same as the contractual rent, namely, Rs. 26 per mensem.

facts.text: Trial court held defendants 1-3 sub-let premises to appellant.

anchor.surface_text: The third issue was whether defendants Nos. 1 to 3 had sublet the premises and the fourth issue was whether there was an assignment in favour of the present appellant by defendants Nos. 1 to 3 of their interest.

facts.text: Trial court rejected partnership contention of defendants 2-3 and assignment claim of appellant.

anchor.surface_text: The trial court held that defendants Nos. 1 to 3 had sub-let the premises to the present appellant and did not accept the contention of defendants Nos. 2 and 3 about partnership or of the appellant about assignment.

facts.text: Trial court dismissed suit for eviction against all four defendants due to amendment of Act in 1959.

anchor.surface_text: Finally the trial court held on the basis of the amendment of the Act in 1959 that there could be no eviction. It therefore dismissed the suit against all the four defendants, namely, the three tenants-in- chief and the appellant so far as eviction was concerned.

facts.text: Trial court ordered tenants-in-chief to pay rent from September 1, 1956 at Rs. 26 per mensem.

anchor.surface_text: It further ordered the tenants-in-chief to pay rent from September 1, 1956 upto date at the rate of Rs. 26 per mensem.

facts.text: Trial court allowed respondents to take deposited rent amount and recover any deficiency from tenants-in-chief.

anchor.surface_text: It further said that the amount of rent had been deposited by the tenants in court and should be taken away by the respondents with the rider that in case the amount fell short the respondents would be at liberty to recover the deficiency if any from the person and property of the tenants-in-chief.

facts.text: Trial court dismissed suit in toto against appellant.

anchor.surface_text: Finally the suit was dismissed in toto against the present appellant.

facts.text: Respondents appealed against dismissal of eviction part.

anchor.surface_text: The respondents then went in appeal against the dismissal of the suit so far as eviction was concerned.

facts.text: Appellate court held no arrears.

anchor.surface_text: On the question of arrears, the appellate court held that there were no arrears.

facts.text: Appellate court held appellant not sub-tenant on his own denial, failed to prove assignment, hence trespasser; ordered ejectment.

anchor.surface_text: But on the other question the appellate court seems to have taken a curious view. It did not examine the correctness of the view taken by the trial court that the present appellant was a sub-tenant. It took the view that as the present appellant had in his written- statement denied that he was a sub-tenant, he could not be a sub-tenant.

facts.text: Appellate court allowed appeal, set aside trial court decree, ordered appellant to hand over possession within six months.

anchor.surface_text: The appellate court therefore allowed the appeal, set aside the decree of the trial court and ordered that the present appellant should hand over possession of the suit premises to the respondents within six months of the order of the appellate court.

facts.text: Appellate court did not order ejectment of tenants-in-chief.

anchor.surface_text: We have said that the view taken by the appellate court was curious because the appellate court does not seem to have ordered the ejectment of the tenants-in-chief.

facts.text: Appellant filed revision under s.115 CPC in Gujarat High Court.

anchor.surface_text: Then followed a revision under s. 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure in the High Court by the present appellant.

facts.text: Tenants-in-chief took no action after appellate court judgment.

anchor.surface_text: It seems that the tenants-in-chief took no action after the judgment of the appellate court, may- be because there was nothing in that judgment which went against them.

facts.text: Gujarat High Court held appellate court not right in setting aside sub-tenant finding without examination.

anchor.surface_text: The High Court held that the appellate court was not right in setting aside the finding that the present appellant was a sub-tenant of the three tenants-in-chief without going into it.

facts.text: High Court held sub-letting finding stood unchallenged, appellant entitled to protection under s.15(2) of Act.

anchor.surface_text: The High Court also seems to have held that in the circumstances the finding of sub-letting stood unchallenged and in view of that finding the present appellant was entitled to contend that he was protected under s. 15  2  of the Act.
